title: BUG on Broadway: Creepy, Brilliant, or Completely Off the Rails? Watch Roma’s Review and Decide
transcript: Good show, hard pass. She calls it straight. Thumbs up, thumbs down, she doesn’t hesitate. Hit or miss, decide before you go. Roma’s Review. Now you know! If anyone could successfully wedge a horror psychological thriller into a love story, it would be Tracy Letts. Bug, which he wrote 30 years ago, is a peculiar play that has aged quite well in our conspiracy-obsessed culture. “You don’t trust me.” “Why do you say that?” “Because you lied to me about having children.” And while I’d have to call it a minor work in Letts’ impressive canon… “How do you know that?” It makes sense to revive it now. Especially with the playwright’s immensely talented wife, Carrie Coon, famed for The White Lotus and The Gilded Age, in the lead role. “I had a child once.” “What happened?” “I lost him.” “He died?” “No, he disappeared.” It starts slow, but thanks in part to the deft hand of director David Cromer, it picks up speed like a ticking time bomb. “You’re gonna call me, you might as well talk. All you do this way is freak me out.” Coon plays 44-year-old Agnes, a waitress in a small Oklahoma City town, with a volatile ex-con ex-husband named Jerry and a fondness for cocaine. “You know I can call the cops. If they trace it to you. You’re busted. No, whatever. I got a gun!” Namir Smallwood is excellent as the mysterious drifter. He’s a perceptive sort and seems well educated, speaking slowly, with a calm demeanor that Agnes finds appealing. “I didn’t mean to freak you out. I was just trying to make a connection or whatever.” Home is a cramped motel room where Agnes lives a pretty sedentary life. That is, until her friend, R.C., brings over a stranger named Peter for a visit. After a violent episode with ex-husband Jerry, Agnes invites Peter to stay over, and the clothes quickly come off. Over the course of close to two hours with an intermission, the story descends into a nightmarish romance. Peter reveals that he escaped from an army hospital, where he had been the subject of crude experiments that turned his blood and body into a parasitic hellscape. Seeing the two of them naked on that stage makes the revelation of bugs planted in his skin all the more cringeworthy. Audience members, including yours truly, were visibly itching body parts. Such is the power of suggestion and effective playwriting. “What are they?” “Aphids. Look around you… They’re in right now. They go in when they feel like it.” “And, uh, tinfoil?” “Scrambles the signal.” There’s a lot more to the story, which ratchets up the suspense, but I won’t spoil it here, other than to say paranoia can be destructively contagious. Coon makes Agnes heartbreakingly plausible. She’s not stupid, she’s starved for connection and protection. “They’re here to kill us. And then send them back out.” Our country’s history of conducting secret experiments on unwitting humans is the backdrop to this story, and it fuels the distrust that leads to the play’s wild ending. The two stars deserve high praise for making a most incredible climax make perfect sense. Bug is likely to stay with you for a while, in part for its wild finish, but also because it’s been given a first-rate production. And Letts wisely injected a healthy dose of humor to keep us engaged. I wouldn’t call it a great play, but it is an admirably combustible one. If you’re looking to get creeped out, it gets the job done. Bug opened January 8th, 2026, at the Samuel J. Friedman Theatre, and it now runs through March 8th. You can get tickets and information at ManhattanTheatreClub.com.
